description_full: DRDGOLD Limited, a gold mining company, engages in the extraction of gold from the retreatment of surface mine tailings in South Africa. The company was formerly known as Durban Roodepoort Deep Limited and changed its name to DRDGOLD Limited in 2004. The company was incorporated in 1895 and is headquartered in Johannesburg, South Africa. DRDGOLD Limited is a subsidiary of Sibanye Gold Proprietary Limited.
ceo_bio: Mr. Daniel Johannes Pretorius B.Proc., L.L.M., LLB | CEO & Executive Director | Age 58 | Compensation: $1.3M (FY2026)
financial_summary: DRDGOLD Limited is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $2.2B market cap on $469M of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +8% over the past three years, a respectable pace for a business of this size. Operating margins are expanding by +7.0pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 39% against a 9% cost of capital — a 31-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 29%.

The business throws off $75M in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.57× so those profits are backed by real cash.
Accruals are elevated at -10.9% of assets, and Sloan showed firms building earnings through accruals rather than cash systematically underperform.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield is only 1.2%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 2.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies

Cyclical sectors like Basic Materials tend to underperform in slowdowns
Late-cycle dynamics increase the probability of a slowdown
Commodity price volatility and cost-curve position — in a downturn only the lowest-cost producer has a business, and the rest carry the overhead.
Environmental remediation liability — tightening regulations on emissions, tailings, and water use create open-ended balance-sheet risk that grows with each legislative cycle.
Trade policy and tariff whiplash — materials producers are first-order casualties of protectionist swings, and margin gets squeezed from both input and output pricing.

sect: Its 37% operating margin runs 27pp above the Basic Materials median (10%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.83x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+10.4% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 35% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 57% and a beta of 0.78, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.50 vs 5y 0.56), so read it loosely.
About $6.3M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 47% in the 2020 crash, 52% in the 2022 bear market and 77% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $18.30 (margin of safety -39%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 15%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $14.84 to $22.89 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
Multiples send mixed signals against Basic Materials peers: cheaper on P/E 8.8 vs 16.5, richer on P/FCF 29.6 vs 22.8 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 14% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.4% (below the risk-free rate).
The Street target $35.00 on average, 37% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 39% clears the cost of capital of 8.7% by 31pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.55).
It runs a 29% gross margin and converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality is mixed: cash conversion of 1.57x, but high accruals (-10.9% of assets).
ROE of 27% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 12pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $73.8M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 8.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 8.1% over 3 years and 10.0% over 5 years, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 17%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 30.0% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 2.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Analysts expect -9.8% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 10%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (6 sales, net $430K sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.2% (4.0% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 18 consecutive years, raising it 48.4% a year over the last five.
